prompt: Which address is outside all three RFC 1918 private ranges?

options.explanation: 10.0.0.0/8 is RFC 1918 private space; everything from 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255 is private.
Correct. 172.16/12 ends at 172.31.255.255. This identifies range membership, not whether 172.32.0.1 is assigned or currently reachable.

workedExample: The RFC 1918 blocks are 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16. The 172.16/12 block spans second octets 16–31, so 172.20.10.5 is inside while 172.32.0.1 is outside. The other options fall in 10/8 and 192.168/16. Address reachability is a separate routing/policy question.

link.title: RFC 1918: Address Allocation for Private Internets

prompt: Two sites each contain a different server at 10.0.5.20 inside 10.0.0.0/16. A VPN joins them into one destination-only routing context. What addressing conflict must be resolved to make both servers unambiguously accessible?

options.text: The VPN MTU is too small; lower the MSS
options.explanation: MTU issues can be path-specific, but changing MSS cannot distinguish two servers with the same destination address in this routing context.

options.text: Overlapping private address space: the same addresses exist on both sides, so routing can't tell which is meant. Renumber one side into a non-overlapping range
options.explanation: Correct. The same destination address names two intended endpoints. Coordinated renumbering removes this ambiguity; translation or separate routing contexts can be alternatives.

options.text: Private addresses can't cross VPNs; switch to public addresses
options.explanation: Private addresses routinely cross VPNs. The problem is that both sides use the *same* private block.
A wider mask makes the overlap worse, not better.

workedExample: Both servers use 10.0.5.20. A destination address alone cannot express which site is intended within the stated shared context. Prefix metrics or equal-cost paths do not create distinct endpoint names. Renumber one side into coordinated, non-overlapping space; alternatively use deliberate translation or separate routing contexts. Merely picking a less familiar private prefix does not guarantee no future overlap.
